The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the finite tuple $Z$ is a Borel random vector with product joint law. For any $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)$, each scalar map $z_j\mapsto u_j\cdot z_j$ is Borel, so preimages of Borel sets lie in $\sigma(Z_j)$. Independence [F1] therefore makes the scalars $u_j\cdot Z_j$ mutually independent. By [A1, F3], each is normal with mean $u_j\cdot a_j$ and variance $u_j^T\Sigma_j u_j$.

For any $s\in\mathbb R$, [F5] and [F4] give $\varphi_{u\cdot Z}(s)=\prod_{j=1}^m\exp\!\left(is\,u_j\cdot a_j-\tfrac12s^2u_j^T\Sigma_j u_j\right)=\exp\!\left(is\,u\cdot a-\tfrac12s^2u^T\Sigma u\right)$. The last expression is the characteristic function of $N_1(u\cdot a,u^T\Sigma u)$ by [F4] in dimension one. Scalar uniqueness [F6] gives $u\cdot Z\sim N_1(u\cdot a,u^T\Sigma u)$, including the zero-variance point-mass case.

The block matrix $\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite because $u^T\Sigma u=\sum_j u_j^T\Sigma_j u_j\ge0$. By [A1, F3], the law $N_D(a,\Sigma)$ exists and its projection laws are the normal laws found in step 2.1. Cramer–Wold [F7] therefore identifies the law of $Z$ with $N_D(a,\Sigma)$. This also covers singular blocks and uses no inverse.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: If $T=0$, then $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$ and $\mu_0$ is the unique asserted law. For $T\ge1$, interleave the coordinate spaces as $D_0=E_0$, $D_{2t-1}=E_t$, and $D_{2t}=F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$. At the transition to $E_t$, define the lifted kernel by $L_{2t-2}(h,A)=K_t(\pi_{t-1}(h),A)$, where $\pi_{t-1}$ selects the $E_{t-1}$ coordinate of the preceding history $h$; at the next transition define $L_{2t-1}(h,B)=G_t(\pi_t(h),B)$, where $\pi_t$ selects the newly adjoined $E_t$ coordinate. These projections are measurable because inverse images of measurable sets are product cylinders. Each lifted section is a probability measure, and each evaluation is measurable by composition, so [F2] makes every lift a probability kernel. After coordinate $D_{2T}$, append singleton spaces with their unit point-mass kernels.

By [A1] and [F3], Ionescu–Tulcea gives a unique probability measure on the countable interleaved product with these lifted kernels. Its marginal on the first $2T+1$ coordinates is a probability measure on $\mathcal Z_T$; the prescribed prefix formula is exactly the displayed iterated integral. The finite product is standard Borel by [F4].

Suppose $Q_T$ is another probability measure on $\mathcal Z_T$ with the same displayed rectangle probabilities. Append the singleton tail to the coordinate tuple by a measurable map and push $Q_T$ forward to the countable product. For any shorter prefix, set all later coordinate sets in the rectangle formula to their whole spaces; the later probability kernels integrate to one, so each shorter marginal is the prescribed iterated integral. Prefixes after $D_{2T}$ add only deterministic singleton coordinates. Ionescu–Tulcea uniqueness [F3] identifies this extension with the measure in step 2.1, so their finite-prefix marginals agree and $Q_T$ equals that marginal. For $T=0$, the formula already fixes $Q_0=\mu_0$.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 treats T=0 explicitly: the path is E_0 and its law is μ_0.
The product-kernel integral allows zero probability on measurable sets and never divides by an event probability, as used in steps 1.1–2.1.
For T=1, step 2.1 gives the prefix law μ_0(dx_0)K_1(x_0,dx_1)G_1(x_1,dy_1).
Dirac initial, transition or observation kernels remain probability kernels and satisfy the same lifted-kernel proof in steps 1.1–2.1.
Step 1.1 handles the initial endpoint and appends singleton tails after the final coordinate D_{2T}.
AC is explicit and is used in steps 2.1–3.1 only through the Ionescu–Tulcea existence and uniqueness theorem.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is an existence-and-uniqueness assertion, not an equivalence.
The theorem is an existence-and-uniqueness assertion, not an equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all three steps and seven cited suppliers. History projections have measurable cylinder preimages and preserve pointwise probability sections; singleton tails provide valid countable kernels for Ionescu–Tulcea under AC. Finite prefixes give existence and the rectangle formula. Appending a measurable deterministic tail to any competitor and setting later rectangles to full spaces gives all shorter prefixes, so the exact uniqueness supplier proves equality. T=0 is handled separately. No empty admissible initial space or density assumption is overlooked.

boundaries.evidence: The definition permits T=0, in which case there are no process or observation noises and the initial Gaussian law remains.
The definition allows zero mean and zero covariance matrices, yielding deterministic Gaussian coordinates.
Definition allows T=1 with one transition, one observation, and positive dimensions.
All P_0,Q_t,R_t may be singular, including zero matrices; no inverse is part of the definition.
Definition starts from x_0 and indexes its equations from t=1 to the finite endpoint T.
Definition assumes AC to realize all positive-semidefinite Gaussian laws; its finite product construction is choice-free.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

spaces. Then:

   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces

product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

derivations.claim: Each Gaussian marginal law in the model exists on its finite-dimensional Euclidean Borel space. Repeatedly applying the finite-product measure construction creates a finite product probability space with these marginals. Its coordinate maps $x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ have the prescribed marginals, and the rectangle formula gives product probabilities on all measurable coordinate rectangles. Therefore the generated sigma-algebras are mutually independent, and the finite family has the product joint law. Thus this space supplies the required independent Gaussian noise vectors.

For a Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_t}$, define $K_t(x,A)=\int 1_A(F_tx+z)\,N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)(dz)$; define $G_t$ analogously using $H_t$ and $N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$. The maps $(x,z)\mapsto F_tx+z$ and $(x,z)\mapsto H_tx+z$ are continuous, so the integrands are product-measurable. Each fixed-state section is a pushforward probability measure. Regard each fixed Gaussian noise law as a constant probability kernel. Kernel integration then makes the evaluations measurable in the state argument, so both families are probability kernels. For fixed $x$ and any $u$, the scalar affine characteristic-function identity applied to $u^Tq_t$, together with the multivariate-normal characteristic-function formula, gives $\mathbb E[e^{iu^T(F_tx+q_t)}]=\exp(iu^TF_tx-\tfrac12u^TQ_tu)$. This is the multivariate-normal characteristic function with mean $F_tx$ and covariance $Q_t$, so its uniqueness identifies the translated law with $N_{d_t}(F_tx,Q_t)$. The same calculation with $H_t,r_t,R_t$ identifies $G_t$. No covariance inverse is used.

Let $\phi$ be any nonnegative Borel function on the finite trajectory space. The recursion is a finite composition of continuous affine maps, so $\phi(Z_T)$ is measurable. By Tonelli, integrate the noise product law from step 1.1 backward, starting with the last pair $(q_T,r_T)$. For each fixed preceding history, the integral over $q_T$ is the pushforward through $x_T=F_Tx_{T-1}+q_T$, hence equals integration against $K_T$; the following integral over $r_T$ is the pushforward through $y_T=H_Tx_T+r_T$, hence equals integration against $G_T$. Repeating this argument for $t=T-1,\ldots,1$ and finally integrating $x_0$ against $\mu_0$ gives $\mathbb E[\phi(Z_T)]=\int\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t)\,\phi(x_0,x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_T,y_T)$. For $T=0$, it is simply integration against $\mu_0$. This is exactly the unique general model law, and the trajectory space is standard Borel.

The stacked-noise lemma gives the vector $W_T$ the multivariate normal law $N(a_T,\Sigma_T)$. Successive substitution in the two recursions shows by finite induction that each coordinate of $Z_T$ is a linear function of $W_T$; collecting those coefficients gives a deterministic matrix $M_T$. For any vector $u$, $u^TZ_T=(M_T^Tu)^TW_T$, whose law is normal with mean $u^TM_Ta_T$ and variance $u^TM_T\Sigma_TM_T^Tu$. The multivariate-normal projection definition gives $Z_T\sim N(M_Ta_T,M_T\Sigma_TM_T^T)$. The covariance is positive semidefinite because $v^T\Sigma_Tv\ge0$ implies $u^TM_T\Sigma_TM_T^Tu=(M_T^Tu)^T\Sigma_T(M_T^Tu)\ge0$. Thus singular covariances are included and no inverse is needed.

boundaries.evidence: For T=0, the product noise vector contains only X_0, the path map is the identity, and the statement reduces to its initial Gaussian law.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all four proof steps, all sixteen direct suppliers, and the source sections. Product coordinate rectangles establish mutual independence; all factors are probabilities and hence sigma-finite. Continuous translations are product-measurable, and the constant probability kernel meets the finite-kernel integration theorem. Characteristic-function uniqueness identifies each shifted Gaussian including null directions. Tonelli permits integration in either order within each independent noise pair and backward elimination gives exactly K_t then G_t. The stacked lemma plus finite linear recursion gives the path matrix and PSD covariance. T=0 gives the identity on x0. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.

Assume AC and fix a finite-horizon model of
[[def-linear-gaussian-state-space-model-with-independent-noises]]. There is a
probability space carrying mutually independent Gaussian vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ with the stated laws. The recursions
$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t$ and $y_t=H_t x_t+r_t$ induce the general kernel-product
law of [[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. In the interleaved order
$Z_T=(x_0,x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_T,y_T)$, there is a deterministic matrix $M_T$
such that
$$Z_T=M_T W_T,\qquad W_T=(x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T),$$
and
$$Z_T\sim N\!\left(M_T a_T,\ M_T\Sigma_T M_T^T\right),\qquad a_T=(m_0,0,\ldots,0),\quad \Sigma_T=\operatorname{diag}(P_0,Q_1,R_1,\ldots,Q_T,R_T).$$
The covariance may be singular.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$, standard-Borel spaces
$E_0,\ldots,E_T$ and $F_1,\ldots,F_T$, an initial probability measure
$\mu_0$ on $E_0$, and transition and observation probability kernels
$K_t:E_{t-1}\to E_t$ and $G_t:E_t\to F_t$ for $1\le t\le T$, as in
[[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]. On the interleaved finite
product space
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
there is a unique probability measure whose rectangle probabilities are the
ordered iterated kernel integrals
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order.
For $T=0$, the assertion is the initial law $\mu_0$ on $E_0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

derivations.claim: By [F10], the degenerate noise satisfies $q_1=0$ almost surely, so both models have $X_1=X_0$ and the same transition kernel $K_1(x,A)=1_A(x)$. Each set of kernels defines the state-space model. The finite-horizon theorem and the path-law theorem supply its joint law. At $x=1$, the two observation-kernel means are $1$ and $2$, so the kernels themselves are distinct.

In the model indexed by $c$, $Y_1=cX_0+r_1$, with both variables centered, $\operatorname{Var}(X_0)=\operatorname{Var}(r_1)=1$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,r_1)=0$ by independence and factorization of expectations. Covariance bilinearity gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,Y_1)=c\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+\operatorname{Cov}(X_0,r_1)=c$. Thus the two joint laws have cross-covariances $1$ and $2$.

Both joint laws have finite second moments. If the laws were equal, the covariance of their first and third coordinates would be equal. Step 1.2 gives different values, so the joint laws are different.

boundaries.reason: The example fixes T=1, one state coordinate and one observation coordinate; an empty horizon is not part of this setup.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 explicitly uses Q_1=0 and the point-mass process noise, with no division by its variance.
The example has exactly one state transition and one observation, as calculated in steps 1.1–1.2.
The zero process-noise covariance is allowed by the definition; both joint laws remain valid by step 1.1.
Step 1.1 identifies the common transition X_0 to X_1 and the observation Y_1 at the final step.
AC is explicit in A1 and is used only through the Gaussian and finite path-law suppliers in step 1.1.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all three verification steps and eleven supplier bodies. Zero-variance q1 is a point mass, so both state paths satisfy X1=X0 and have identical initial/transition laws. At x=1 the observation normals have distinct means, but the proof also checks actual joint laws rather than relying on pointwise kernel differences alone. The fixed scalar one-step construction needs no density, inversion, conditioning version or additional choice; AC is inherited from Gaussian/path results. No reader/refuter defect applies.
